# Assignment

::: {.section-art}
{{< lif "../../icons/contacts.json" state=in-reveal colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}}
:::

## Assignment {.fs80}

::: {.columns .pv4}
::: {.column width="60%"}
-   It helps to store data in [named objects]{.b .green}
    -   This makes the data easier to use and re-use
    -   And the code easier to write and read

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   Which command is easier to follow?
    1.  Dial *7 8 5 8 6 4 0 8 4 1*
    2.  Call *Office Phone*
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   Named objects come from [assignment]{.b .blue}
    -   Give a **name** then an **arrow** then the **data**
:::
:::

::: {.column .tc .pv5 width="40%"}
::: {.fragment}
`office <- 7858640841`
:::
:::
:::

## Assigning and Printing

```{r}
#| echo: true

# Store the value 2 under the name x
x <- 2

# Typing the name on its own prints the value
x
```

::: {.takeaway}
`<-` stores a value under a name. Assigning prints nothing; typing the name on
its own is how you ask R to show you what it holds.
:::

## Using an Object in Math

```{r}
#| echo: true

# Once x exists, it stands in for its value
x * 4

# It can appear as many times as you like in one line
(10 + x - 1) / x
```

::: {.takeaway}
Wherever a value could go, a name holding that value can go instead, as often
as you need it.
:::

## Updating Requires Assignment

```{r}
#| echo: true

# Using x does not change it
x + 1

# x is still 2
x
```

```{r}
#| echo: true

# To update it, assign the result back to the name
x <- x + 1
x
```

::: {.takeaway}
Using an object never changes it. To update one, assign the result **back to the
same name**.
:::

## Objects Can Create Other Objects

```{r}
#| echo: true

# The right-hand side can use objects that already exist
y <- 10 + x
y

# And a line can use several objects at once
y / x
```

::: {.takeaway}
The right-hand side of `<-` is just an expression, so it can use any objects that
already exist. That is how a script builds up from one line to the next.
:::

# Naming

::: {.section-art}
{{< lif "../../icons/business_card.json" state=in-reveal colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}}
:::

## Naming {.fs80}

-   Object names can [only include]{.b .blue}:
    -   Letters: `a-Z`
    -   Numbers: `0-9`
    -   Underscores: `_`
    -   Periods: `.`

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   Additional Rules:
    -   Must [start with a letter]{.b .blue} (or a period)
    -   Cannot contain spaces or dashes
    -   Cannot contain other symbols
    -   Names are case-sensitive (`age` ≠ `Age`)
:::

## Good Names are a Balancing Act

```{r}
#| echo: true

x <- 93 # legal, but what is it?

rate <- 93 # too short to be clear

heart_rate_in_beats_per_minute <- 93 # too long to type

heart_rate_bpm <- 93 # just right
```

::: {.takeaway}
A good name is the shortest one a reader can still understand six months later.
:::

## Pitfall: No Spaces or Dashes

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-line-numbers: false

heart rate <- 93
```

::: {.r-error}
```
Error: unexpected symbol in "heart rate"
```
:::

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| error: true
#| code-line-numbers: false

heart-rate <- 93
```

::: {.takeaway}
A space stops R mid-line. A dash is worse: R reads `heart-rate` as *heart minus
rate*, so it fails looking for an object rather than telling you the name is
illegal. Use an underscore: `heart_rate`.
:::

## Pitfall: No Special Symbols

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| error: true
#| code-line-numbers: false

age@time2 <- 12
```

```{r}
#| echo: true

age_time2 <- 12 # correct
age_time2
```

::: {.takeaway}
`@` already means something else in R, so it reads `age@time2` as an operation on
an object called `age`. Letters, numbers, `_` and `.` are all a name may hold.
:::

## Pitfall: Names Must Start with a Letter

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-line-numbers: false

1_heart_rate <- 93
```

::: {.r-error}
```
Error: unexpected input in "1_"
```
:::

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-line-numbers: false

_heart_rate <- 93
```

::: {.r-error}
```
Error: unexpected symbol in "_heart_rate"
```
:::

```{r}
#| echo: true

heart_rate_1 <- 93 # correct: the digit comes last
heart_rate_1
```

::: {.takeaway}
Move the digit to the end and the name is fine.
:::

## Names are Case-Sensitive

```{r}
#| echo: true

heart_rate <- 93
Heart_rate <- 88

# These are two entirely different objects
heart_rate
Heart_rate
```

::: {.takeaway}
One capital letter makes an entirely different object. R will not warn you, because it
has no way to know you meant the other one.
:::

# Functions

::: {.section-art}
{{< lif "../../icons/gears.json" state=in-reveal colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}}
:::

## Functions {.fs80}

::: {.columns .pv4}
::: {.column width="60%"}
-   [Recipes]{.b .green} allow chefs to cook up tasty treats
    -   Recipes call for ingredients
    -   Recipes involve one or more steps
    -   Steps transform ingredients into treats

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   [Functions]{.b .blue} are like *customizable* recipes
    -   Functions call for inputs ("arguments")
    -   Functions involve one or more lines
    -   Code transforms inputs into outputs
    -   Functions usually need parentheses
:::
:::

::: {.column .tc .pv5 width="40%"}
::: {.fragment}
`out <- f(in1, in2)`
:::
:::
:::

## Functions Do a Task More Readably

::: {.f5}
`output <- function_name(input)`
:::

```{r}
#| echo: true

# The hard way
9 ^ (1 / 2)

# The readable way
x <- sqrt(9)
x
```

::: {.takeaway}
A function gives a name to something you would otherwise have to spell out. It is
easier to write, and far easier to read back.
:::

## What Can Go Inside a Function

```{r}
#| echo: true

y <- 9

# The input can be an object rather than a literal value
sqrt(y)

# Or the result of a calculation
round(2 / 3)
```

::: {.takeaway}
Anything that produces a value can go in the input slot: a literal, an object,
or another calculation. R works out the inside first, then hands the result over.
:::

## Arguments Customize a Function

::: {.f5}
`output <- function_name(argument, argument_name = argument_value)`
:::

```{r}
#| echo: true

round(2 / 3, digits = 2)

# digits has a default of 0, so this...
round(2 / 3)

# ...means exactly the same thing as this
round(2 / 3, digits = 0)
```

::: {.takeaway}
Extra arguments change *how* a function does its job. Most have a default, which
is what you get when you leave them out.
:::

# Vectors

::: {.section-art}
{{< lif "../../icons/stack_list.json" state=in-reveal colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}}
:::

## Vectors {.fs70}

::: {.columns .pv4}
::: {.column width="60%"}
-   [Vectors]{.b .blue} combine similar objects into a collection
    -   *I like to imagine a train pulling multiple cars*<br />
    ![](../../img/traincar.png)
    -   A vector is one object with many sub-objects
    -   We refer to each sub-object as an [element]{.b .green}

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   Some functions [transform each element]{.b .green} in turn
    -   *Double the amount of cargo in every train car*
:::

::: {.fragment .mt1}
-   Some functions [summarize across elements]{.b .green}
    -   *Calculate the total cargo across all train cars*
:::
:::

::: {.column .tc .pv5 width="40%"}
::: {.fragment}
`v <- c(1, 2, 3)`
:::

:::
:::


## Combining Elements into a Vector

::: {.f5}
`vector_name <- c(element1, element2, element3)`
:::

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
#| code-line-numbers: false

x <- 4 9 16 25
```

::: {.r-error}
```
Error: unexpected numeric constant in "x <- 4 9"
```
:::

```{r}
#| echo: true

x <- c(4, 9, 16, 25)
x

y <- c(2, 3)
y
```

::: {.takeaway}
Elements must be separated by commas and wrapped in `c()`. Without it R sees
several values where it expected one.
:::

## Combining Vectors and Elements

```{r}
#| echo: true

# c() also joins whole vectors together
c(x, y)

# And vectors and single elements
c(x, y, 20)
```

::: {.takeaway}
`c()` flattens whatever you give it into one vector, so there is no such thing as
a vector nested inside another.
:::

## Math Transforms Each Element

```{r}
#| echo: true

x + 1

x * 3

# But as before, nothing is saved without assignment
x
```

::: {.takeaway}
An operation applies to **every element at once**, with no loop to write. As with
a single value, the result is not saved unless you assign it.
:::

## Functions That Transform

```{r}
#| echo: true

sqrt(x)

log(x)
```

::: {.takeaway}
These return a vector as long as the input: one answer per element.
:::

## Functions That Summarize

```{r}
#| echo: true

length(x)

sum(x)

mean(x)
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| error: true

average(x)
```

::: {.takeaway}
These collapse the whole vector to a single number. Note the last one: R names
this function `mean()`, and a reasonable guess is still an error.
:::

## Pitfall: Missing Values are Contagious

```{r}
#| echo: true

scores <- c(10, 12, 20, NA, 8)

# NA spreads: the mean depends on the value we do not have
mean(scores)

# Ask for the mean of the non-missing values instead
mean(scores, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.takeaway}
`NA` means "we do not know", so any answer depending on it is also unknown. That
is a feature, not a bug. `na.rm = TRUE` answers from what you have.
:::
